newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong says ready to defend dollar from attack.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong says ready to defend dollar from attack.

text.p: Hong Kong authorities punched home on Wednesday that the territory stands ready to face down any speculative attack on its currency.

"As the lender of last resort for Hong Kong dollars, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) will not lend cheaply, directly or indirectly to speculators," Joseph Yam, chief executive of the territory's de facto central bank said.

Hong Kong's dollar is pegged at HK$7.8 to the U.S. dollar, and the currency is being watched closely for any signs of weakness due to uncertainty ahead of the British colony's handover to Chinese rule next year.
Echoing comments made in London last week, Yam said Hong Kong's hefty foreign exchange reserves of US$60 billion will hold the peg through any speculative assault.

"For as long as those holding Hong Kong dollar assets remain confident in the currency, there is very little that speculators without Hong Kong dollar assets can do in the market to destabilize our currency and make a profit," Yam said.

Speculators would have to borrow to cover short Hong Kong dollar positions, and Yam expressed the hope that private commercial banks would resist requests for Hong Kong dollar loans by hedge funds or others involved in an attack.
"I expect financial institutions serving as lenders of first rsort to borrowers will also not fund speculators cheaply and expose themselves to the risks of a funding squeeze," he said.
Yam also does not expect to have to call upon a repurchase agreement with the People's Bank of China, which held foreign reserves in excess of US$93 billion at the end of August.

"The PBOC has indicated that if there were to be a need, China's foreign currency reserves could be used to support the Hong Kong dollar, although I wish and I am confident that we would not come to that," Yam said.

He also repeated comments that Hong Kong will retain its own currency and monetary independence well beyond Hong Kong's transformation into a special administrative region under Chinese sovereignty next year.
"China has taken the very helpful view, in defining the relationship between the two monetary systems, that they are to be 'mutually independent,'" Yam said.
One system will not take precedence over another and assets and liabilities between the two monetary systems are to be considered foreign assets and liabilities, he said.

Yam also reaffirmed the continuation of the Hong Kong dollar peg to the United States currency and rejected any suggestion that it would be replaced by a peg to the yuan once the Chinese currency becomes fully convertible.
"We need monetary segregation and not monetary union in whatever form," Yam said.
A single currency or fixed relationship might make sense for trading partners such as the European Community, where countries emjoy a similar stage of economic and social development.
But even the EU has had difficulty establishing convergence criteria, and so far, only one country qualifies.
"I really cannot find any other two economies which are more different than those of China and Hong Kong," Yam said.
This ensures that the Hong Kong dollar will continue to exist as the legal tender of Hong Kong well beyond the handover at midnight on June 30 next year, he said.
